# Train-the-Trainer — Delivering Eduversal PD Consistently

> **Read `_facilitator-conventions.md` first.** This guide assumes you know the shared playbook — because your job is to *deliver* it consistently and to *coach others* to deliver it.

---

## Why this session exists

Eduversal Specialists, Coordinators, and Directors will deliver the PD sessions in `docs/pd/` to teachers and leaders across many partner schools. The risk is **drift**: the same session lands very differently depending on who runs it. One Specialist over-talks; another skips the activity; a third changes the message. When that happens, a teacher in School A and a teacher in School B do not get the same Eduversal.

This session prepares trainers to deliver **consistently**: same message, same structure, same quality — adapted to each room, but never drifting from the core. It is the session that protects every other session.

---

## Who this is for

- **Eduversal Subject Specialists** — the main deliverers. They visit schools and run subject-relevant PD.
- **Coordinators** — who run cross-functional sessions.
- **Directors** — who set the standard and coach the Specialists.

(Note: in the competency framework, these roles share the **specialists track** — 6 domains × 29 competencies — including **COF** *Classroom Observation & Feedback* and **TPD** *Teacher Professional Development*, which are exactly the competencies a good trainer needs.)

---

## Learning objectives

By the end of this session, each trainer can:

1. **Deliver** any session in this corpus using the five timing blocks, keeping input short and activity long.
2. **Adapt** a session for a strong room and a struggling room without changing the core message.
3. **Model** the ESL/EAL delivery rules (because they are training ESL/EAL educators).
4. **Hold** the same message across schools — so the network gets one Eduversal, not fifteen.

---

## Materials & setup

- This whole `docs/pd/` corpus (every trainer should have read it).
- One full session guide to practise delivering (e.g. `../teachers/session-appraisal-for-teachers.md`).
- A short "delivery rubric" — what good delivery looks like (below).
- Video or live practice slots.

**Face-to-face:** a half-day; trainers practise delivering short segments to each other.
**Online:** same, in breakout rooms; record practice segments for feedback.

---

## Run-of-show (modular half-day — adapt to your group)

| Block | Time | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **1. The why** | 25 min | Why consistency matters: one Eduversal across 15 schools. The drift problem. |
| **2. The shape** | 30 min | The five timing blocks (§2). Why input is short and activity is long. Walk one session's run-of-show. |
| **3. ESL/EAL delivery** | 30 min | Model the §1 rules. Practise glossing a term, giving thinking time, checking understanding (not agreement). |
| **4. Practice — deliver a segment** | 60 min | Each trainer delivers one 10-minute segment of a real session to the group. Peers give Glow/Grow/Go. |
| **5. Adapting without drifting** | 25 min | How to flex for a strong vs struggling room while holding the core message + citations. |
| **6. Consistency commitments** | 20 min | Agree the non-negotiables every trainer will hold. Exit ticket. |

---

## The core message: deliver consistently

**The non-negotiables every Eduversal trainer holds** (agree these as a group in block 6):

1. **Keep the five blocks.** Welcome → Input → Activity → Debrief → Close. Never cut the activity to "finish the slides".
2. **Input stays short.** If you are talking for more than 25% of the session, stop and give them something to do. (`_facilitator-conventions.md` §2; EEF Effective PD 2021.)
3. **Hold the message.** The citations are the message. Do not replace the framework content with personal opinion. If you disagree with a framework, raise it with Eduversal — do not teach a different version in the room.
4. **Model ESL/EAL.** Short sentences. Gloss jargon. Thinking time. You are training people who teach in English as an additional language — your delivery must show the rules you are teaching. (`_facilitator-conventions.md` §1.)
5. **Use Glow / Grow / Go on yourselves.** After every delivery, one strength, one growth, one next step. Trainers improve the same way teachers do.

---

## Facilitator talking points (for the Director / lead trainer)

**On consistency vs control.** *"Consistency is not reading a script. It is holding the same message and structure while reading the room. A good trainer adapts the examples to the school in front of them — but never changes what F2 measures or what the red lines are."*

**On the drift problem.** *"If one Specialist says appraisal is 'mostly paperwork' and another says it is 'mostly the lesson', teachers get two different Eduversals. The citations exist so we all say the same true thing. F2 is 50%. That is not an opinion to soften."* (`appraisal-framework-v2.json → weights`).

**On modelling ESL/EAL.** *"You are training people who think in Bahasa before they speak in English. If you speak fast, in long sentences, with unglossed jargon — you have failed the session before the content even lands. Model the rules. Be the example."*

**On the trainer's own competency.** *"Delivering PD well is itself a competency — COF (Classroom Observation & Feedback) and TPD (Teacher Professional Development) in your specialists framework. Treat your own delivery as something you grow, with evidence, like any other competency."* (`competency_framework/specialists` → domains `cof`, `tpd`).

---

## Activity: deliver a segment (60 min)

Each trainer picks a **10-minute segment** from a real session guide (an input block, an activity set-up, or a debrief). They deliver it to the group as if the group were teachers. The group then gives **Glow / Grow / Go**:

- **Glow** — one specific thing that worked (evidence, not "good job").
- **Grow** — one specific thing to improve (tied to the delivery rubric).
- **Go** — one concrete change for next time.

**Delivery rubric (what the group watches for):**
- Did the input stay short and concrete?
- Did the activity get clear instructions (and an online variant if needed)?
- Was the language ESL/EAL — short sentences, glossed terms, thinking time?
- Did the trainer check understanding (not just agreement)?
- Did the message stay faithful to the source (no drift)?

- **Online:** breakout rooms of 3; record each segment; the group reviews together.

> **Why this works:** trainers cannot learn consistency by hearing about it. They learn it by delivering, getting specific feedback, and trying again — exactly the practice-based PD we ask of teachers.

---

## Common questions (answer in simple English)

**"Can I change the examples to fit my subject / school?"**
Yes — and you should. Adapt the *examples* to the room. Do not change the *message* or the *citations*. Same truth, local examples.

**"What if a session is too long for my time slot?"**
Cut the input, never the activity. You can shorten the talking. You cannot remove the doing — that is where learning happens.

**"What if a teacher asks something I cannot answer?"**
Say so honestly, and find the answer in the References Hub or ask Eduversal. "I will check and come back to you" builds more trust than a confident wrong answer. Never say "just try it" for anything that has a red line (especially AI in coursework).

**"How do we stay consistent across 15 schools?"**
Same corpus, same structure, same non-negotiables (above), and Glow/Grow/Go on each other after sessions. Consistency is a habit the trainers hold together, not a rule imposed from outside.

---

## Exit ticket

1. One delivery habit I will hold every time.
2. One thing I will adapt for my schools (without changing the message).
3. One thing I am still unsure about.

> Collect line 3 — it tells the Director where the trainer team needs more support before going out to schools.
